facts.title: Sale of Elvis Presley's Contract (1955)
facts.body: In 1955, Sun Records sold Elvis Presley's contract to RCA Records for $35,000. This sum represented the highest amount ever paid for a recording artist's contract at that time. Sam Phillips initially set the price intending it as an "absurd amount" to bluff Tom Parker into refusal, hoping to retain Elvis. "But in 1955 that would be the highest sum of money ever paid for a recording artist's contract."

facts.title: Search for an "Elvis Equivalent" (1955)
facts.body: Despite Ken Nelson's lack of understanding of rockabilly, he recognized Capitol Records' need to find its own answer to Elvis Presley. facts.title: Sailor Career and Motorcycle Accident (1955)
facts.body: Gene Vincent, born Vincent Eugene Craddock, had been content with his career as a sailor until 1955. After reenlisting and receiving a $900 bonus, he purchased a Triumph racing motorbike. This bike was involved in an accident that severely damaged his left leg. The official story attributed the crash to a woman driving a Chrysler, while another account suggested Vincent crashed trying to ride under a naval base security barrier while intoxicated. The accident left his leg shattered, causing chronic osteomyelitis, a permanent open sore, and frequent bone fractures, leading to lifelong pain. He adamantly refused amputation, opting for over a year in a cast followed by a metal brace. "Whatever the truth, his left leg was smashed up, and looked for a long time like it was going to be amputated, but he refused to allow this."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Elvis Presley Inspiration (1955)
facts.body: Following his discharge from the naval hospital in September 1955, Gene Vincent attended a country music show headlined by Hank Snow, which also featured the Louvin Brothers. However, it was witnessing a young Elvis Presley perform lower down the bill that profoundly changed Vincent's life, inspiring him to pursue a career in rock and roll. "The story seems to be the same for almost every one of the early rockabilly artists... he immediately decides that he wants to do that, that Elvis is doing something that's like what the young man has already started doing, but he's proved that you can do it on stage for people."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: UK Tour as Part of Exchange (1955)

facts.body: The idea for this landmark song originated from Johnny Cash's anecdote about a serviceman referring to his shoes, and was solidified when Perkins overheard an audience member exclaim, "Don't step on my suede!" Perkins wrote the song one night, playing his electric guitar unplugged to avoid disturbing his wife. He recorded it on December 19, 1955, and famously misspelled "suede" as "SWAD-A-D-E" because he did not know the correct spelling. The song became a massive cross-over hit, reaching number two on both Pop and Country charts and number five on the R&B chart. Perkins's version is rhythmically sophisticated, featuring a stop-time introduction that transitions from 6/4 time into 4/4, creating a unique tension and release dynamic. "Perkins found himself one night getting out of bed, playing his electric guitar unplugged, so as not to disturb his wife, and writing a song he called Blue Suede shoes."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

The movie was intended to warn against juvenile delinquency, but the song's inclusion famously led to kids dancing in theaters, sometimes resulting in violence and vandalism. facts.body: This song was originally written by Book Ram with the intention of giving it to The Ink Spots, but it was set aside. Book Ram initially thought the song was "rubbish," an assessment seemingly confirmed by the initial bad recording by The Platters. Jean Bennett, Ram's assistant, rediscovered the sheet music, and Tony Williams insisted on recording it. A voice crack by Williams on the word "only" during an early take was incorporated, adding to the song's character. It became a massive hit, defining an era as the epitome of 1950s Smooth Balladry, spending 30 weeks on the R&B chart (seven at number one) and 22 weeks on the pop chart (peaking at number five). Federal Records rush-released their "awful" original recording to cash in, leading to a lawsuit with Ram and Mercury, which Federal eventually won the right to release but it didn't chart. "no, it sounded good, use it."

facts.title: Blackboard Jungle Audience Reaction (1955)
facts.body: The 1955 film *Blackboard Jungle*, intended to warn about juvenile delinquency, ironically attracted delinquents and wannabes. When Bill Haley and the Comets' "Rock Around the Clock" played, kids would stand up and dance in theaters, occasionally leading to violence and vandalism. The movie was subsequently banned in many cities and throughout the UK due to this disruptive audience behavior. "The movie was supposed to warn of the growing danger of juvenile delinquency. Instead, it attracted delinquents and delinquent wannabes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Chrysler Highway Hi-Fi Turntable (1955)
facts.body: Introduced in 1955, the Highway Hi-Fi was a factory-installed, under-dash turntable available in certain Chrysler and DeSoto models, costing an additional $200 (over $2,000 in today's money). Designed by Dr. Peter Goldmark (who also helped develop the 33 1/3 LP), it played special 7-inch, 16 2/3 RPM ultra-microgrove records, offering up to 45 minutes per side. However, sound quality was awful, and the tone arm frequently skipped due to 1950s car suspension, especially while in motion, despite being in a shockproof cabinet. Attempts to add weight to the tone arm to prevent skipping ultimately destroyed the records. Content was limited, sold only at Chrysler dealerships, and exclusively provided by Columbia Records, with no rock and roll due to CBS head William Paley's dislike of the genre. The system was a flop, selling only about 4,000 units before discontinuation, partly due to CBS owning radio stations and seeing it as a threat, as well as being distracted by television. "The original Highway High Five was pretty much doomed from the start."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Philco's First Battery-Powered Turntable (1955)
facts.body: In 1955, Philco, a Philadelphia-based battery company, introduced the first transistor-based, battery-powered turntable. This innovation allowed users to play their 33-30 LPs, 45 RPM singles, and 78s anywhere, as it did not require a power outlet. It featured a built-in, powerful amplifier, a "modern-ish" speaker, and a volume control, retailing for $59.95 US (equivalent to nearly $750 today), offering unprecedented convenience for its time. `"It wasn't until 1955, when Philco, the Philadelphia-based battery company, put out a transistor-based battery-powered turn table on sale."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: 1955 Record Prices
facts.body: In 1955, an album could cost up to $6 (approximately $53 today), while a 45 RPM single cost around 89 cents (almost $8 today). "Back in 1955, you could expect to spend up to $6 for an album, which is about $53 in today's money. And a 45? Well, that cost is a little 89 cents or almost $8 today."

facts.title: Early Electronic Music Example: Drip City (1955)
facts.body: The track "Drip City" from 1955 showcases the capabilities of Hugh Le Caine's Electronic Sackbut. For this piece, Le Caine processed the sound of a single water drip through his invention to create one of the earliest examples of keyboard-generated electronic music. "He took the sound of a single drip of water and ran it through his electronic Sack Butte."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott (December 1955)
facts.body: Initiated after Rosa Parks' refusal to give up her seat, the Montgomery Bus Boycott was organized by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in response to the inhumanity of segregated bus seating. Black people were required to pay the same fares as white people but had to sit at the back, only if all white seats were taken, and had to stand if a white person was standing. King rallied the community with the statement, "This is inhuman. We will boycott your bus system," which he viewed as the most passive political act. "Dr. King decided that in Montgomery, Alabama, black people had to pay the same prices on the buses as white people, but we had to sit in the back. And we could only sit in the back if every available seat was taken by a white person."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Vinyl Production (1955-1960)
facts.body: Over two million unique albums, meaning unique recordings that came to market, were produced between 1955 and 1960, a period identified as the "golden age of music." Of these, it's estimated that less than 5% hold any value today (even as little as one dollar or euro), with the rest considered worthless. "en esa época se han producido más de dos millones de álbumes, no dos millones de discos de Vinilo, no dos millones de álbumes únicos, o sea, grabaciones, que han salido al mercado."

facts.title: History of Rock Music Genre Blending (1955)
facts.body: By the end of 1955, the distinctions between rock and roll, rhythm and blues, and country music were not hard and fast. The history of popular music genres shows that they eventually encompass each other, as exemplified by artists like Johnny Cash who bridged these styles. "at the end of 1955, in particular, there was no hard and fast distinction between the genres of rock and roll, rhythm and blues and country music."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Civil Rights Struggle Context (1955-1956)
facts.body: The mid-1950s represented a pivotal and volatile period in the civil rights struggle, marked by significant events such as the murder of Emmett Till in August 1955, Rosa Parks' refusal to yield her seat in December 1955, and escalating white supremacist terrorism, including the firebombing of churches and the homes of civil rights leaders like Dr. Martin Luther King. This social ferment provided a crucial backdrop for understanding the revolutionary nature of rock and roll at the time. "The murder of Emmett Till, supposedly for whistling at a white woman, had been in August 1955."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Recent Innovation (1955)
facts.body: The Fender Stratocaster was a recent innovation in 1955, noted for its tremolo arm, which Buddy Holly's friend Joe B. Mauldin humorously referred to as a "gear shift." "Holly's friend Joe B. Mouldin said of the Strat that it was the first instrument he'd ever seen with a gear shift. He was referring there to the tremolo arm on the guitar, a recent innovation that had only been brought in that year."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Purchase by Buddy Holly (1955)
facts.body: Buddy Holly was able to purchase his own Fender Stratocaster in 1955, along with an amp and stage suit, thanks to a $1000 loan from bass player Larry Wellborn, marking a significant step in his musical career. "Lent him $1000, a massive amount of money in 1955, so he could buy himself a friend of Stratocaster, an amp, and a stage suit."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Musicians' Union Protectionist Agreement (1930s-1955)
facts.body: From the early 1930s until 1955, the American Federation of Musicians and the British Musicians Union maintained a mutual protectionist agreement. This arrangement prevented musicians from one country from performing in the other, a policy implemented after the Duke Ellington band's UK tour in 1933. While individual non-instrumental performers could sometimes cross borders if they employed local musicians (e.g., Ray Noble and Al Bowley hiring Glenn Miller in the US, Johnny Ray hiring British musicians in the UK), full bands were restricted. "Both the American Federation of Musicians and their British equivalent, the Musicians Union, had, since the early 1930s, had a mutual protectionist agreement which prevented musicians from one of the countries playing in the other."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: "One-In, One-Out" Union Agreement (1955-Decades)
facts.body: In 1955, the American Federation of Musicians and the British Musicians Union revised their protectionist agreement to a "one-in, one-out" policy, which lasted for several decades. This new rule allowed musicians from each country to tour, but only as a direct, reciprocal swap. Examples include Louis Armstrong touring the UK if Freddie Randall toured the US, and Stan Kenton's band touring the UK in exchange for the Ted Heath Orchestra touring the US. "In 1955, the two unions finally came to a one-in, one-out agreement, which would last for the next few decades, where musicians from each country could tour, but only as a alike for like swap."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: 1955 Record Prices
facts.body: In 1955, an album could cost up to $6 (approximately $53 today), while a 45 RPM single cost around 89 cents (almost $8 today). "Back in 1955, you could expect to spend up to $6 for an album, which is about $53 in today's money. And a 45? Well, that cost is a little 89 cents or almost $8 today."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Blackboard Jungle Audience Reaction (1955)
facts.body: The 1955 film *Blackboard Jungle*, intended to warn about juvenile delinquency, ironically attracted delinquents and wannabes. When Bill Haley and the Comets' "Rock Around the Clock" played, kids would stand up and dance in theaters, occasionally leading to violence and vandalism. The movie was subsequently banned in many cities and throughout the UK due to this disruptive audience behavior. "The movie was supposed to warn of the growing danger of juvenile delinquency. Instead, it attracted delinquents and delinquent wannabes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Chrysler Highway Hi-Fi Turntable (1955)
facts.body: Introduced in 1955, the Highway Hi-Fi was a factory-installed, under-dash turntable available in certain Chrysler and DeSoto models, costing an additional $200 (over $2,000 in today's money). Designed by Dr. Peter Goldmark (who also helped develop the 33 1/3 LP), it played special 7-inch, 16 2/3 RPM ultra-microgrove records, offering up to 45 minutes per side. However, sound quality was awful, and the tone arm frequently skipped due to 1950s car suspension, especially while in motion, despite being in a shockproof cabinet. Attempts to add weight to the tone arm to prevent skipping ultimately destroyed the records. Content was limited, sold only at Chrysler dealerships, and exclusively provided by Columbia Records, with no rock and roll due to CBS head William Paley's dislike of the genre. The system was a flop, selling only about 4,000 units before discontinuation, partly due to CBS owning radio stations and seeing it as a threat, as well as being distracted by television. "The original Highway High Five was pretty much doomed from the start."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Civil Rights Struggle Context (1955-1956)
facts.body: The mid-1950s represented a pivotal and volatile period in the civil rights struggle, marked by significant events such as the murder of Emmett Till in August 1955, Rosa Parks' refusal to yield her seat in December 1955, and escalating white supremacist terrorism, including the firebombing of churches and the homes of civil rights leaders like Dr. Martin Luther King. This social ferment provided a crucial backdrop for understanding the revolutionary nature of rock and roll at the time. "The murder of Emmett Till, supposedly for whistling at a white woman, had been in August 1955."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: History of Rock Music Genre Blending (1955)
facts.body: By the end of 1955, the distinctions between rock and roll, rhythm and blues, and country music were not hard and fast. The history of popular music genres shows that they eventually encompass each other, as exemplified by artists like Johnny Cash who bridged these styles. "at the end of 1955, in particular, there was no hard and fast distinction between the genres of rock and roll, rhythm and blues and country music."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott (December 1955)
facts.body: Initiated after Rosa Parks' refusal to give up her seat, the Montgomery Bus Boycott was organized by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in response to the inhumanity of segregated bus seating. Black people were required to pay the same fares as white people but had to sit at the back, only if all white seats were taken, and had to stand if a white person was standing. King rallied the community with the statement, "This is inhuman. We will boycott your bus system," which he viewed as the most passive political act. "Dr. King decided that in Montgomery, Alabama, black people had to pay the same prices on the buses as white people, but we had to sit in the back. And we could only sit in the back if every available seat was taken by a white person."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Philco's First Battery-Powered Turntable (1955)
facts.body: In 1955, Philco, a Philadelphia-based battery company, introduced the first transistor-based, battery-powered turntable. This innovation allowed users to play their 33-30 LPs, 45 RPM singles, and 78s anywhere, as it did not require a power outlet. It featured a built-in, powerful amplifier, a "modern-ish" speaker, and a volume control, retailing for $59.95 US (equivalent to nearly $750 today), offering unprecedented convenience for its time. `"It wasn't until 1955, when Philco, the Philadelphia-based battery company, put out a transistor-based battery-powered turn table on sale."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Vinyl Production (1955-1960)
facts.body: Over two million unique albums, meaning unique recordings that came to market, were produced between 1955 and 1960, a period identified as the "golden age of music." Of these, it's estimated that less than 5% hold any value today (even as little as one dollar or euro), with the rest considered worthless. "en esa época se han producido más de dos millones de álbumes, no dos millones de discos de Vinilo, no dos millones de álbumes únicos, o sea, grabaciones, que han salido al mercado."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Early Electronic Music Example: Drip City (1955)
facts.body: The track "Drip City" from 1955 showcases the capabilities of Hugh Le Caine's Electronic Sackbut. For this piece, Le Caine processed the sound of a single water drip through his invention to create one of the earliest examples of keyboard-generated electronic music. "He took the sound of a single drip of water and ran it through his electronic Sack Butte."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Recent Innovation (1955)
facts.body: The Fender Stratocaster was a recent innovation in 1955, noted for its tremolo arm, which Buddy Holly's friend Joe B. Mauldin humorously referred to as a "gear shift." "Holly's friend Joe B. Mouldin said of the Strat that it was the first instrument he'd ever seen with a gear shift. He was referring there to the tremolo arm on the guitar, a recent innovation that had only been brought in that year."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
